references.text: Fulfillment of the prophecy: The fish in the Nile died, and the river stank so that the Egyptians could not drink its water.
The psalmist recalls how God turned Egypt's waters into blood and killed their fish.
Isaiah prophesies that the fishermen by the Nile will mourn, reflecting God's judgment on Egypt's water sources.
Ezekiel uses the image of fish in the Nile in his judgment against Pharaoh and Egypt, recalling the plagues.
In Revelation, a third of the creatures in the sea die when the sea turns to blood, paralleling Egypt's plague.
The bowls of wrath turn the sea and rivers into blood, and all life within them dies—an eschatological parallel to Egypt's plague.
Prophetic fulfillment and thematic parallel: The historical plague in Exodus foreshadows the prophesied destruction of Egypt's economy and livelihood in Isaiah.
Theological contrast: Jeremiah's image of Egypt's hubris (the Nile as a warrior) stands in sharp opposition to Exodus' portrayal of the Nile as a powerless victim of God's judgment.
Direct narrative connection: Verse 24 describes the concrete consequence of the judgment proclaimed in verse 18.
Prophetic precursor: The sign in Exodus 4 foreshadows the mechanism and content of the plague itself described in Exodus 7.
Theological opposition: Ezekiel exposes Egypt's hubris (their belief that they own the Nile), while Exodus demonstrates that God actually owns and rules over it.
